title.en: Equilibrium with free entry and exit

body.en: If firms earn super-normal profit, new firms enter, market supply rises and price falls. If firms make losses, some exit, supply falls and price rises. *Entry and exit* stop only when each firm earns normal profit, that is when price equals minimum average cost: $p = \min AC$. Each firm produces the output at which AC is minimum, and the number of firms is $n = q^D(\min AC)/q_{\text{firm}}$.

points.en: Long run: p = min AC, normal profit

narration.en: Free entry and exit push price to the minimum of average cost, where firms earn only normal profit. The number of firms adjusts to meet demand.
narration.kn: ಮುಕ್ತ ಪ್ರವೇಶ ಮತ್ತು ನಿರ್ಗಮನವು ಬೆಲೆಯನ್ನು ಕನಿಷ್ಠ ಸರಾಸರಿ ವೆಚ್ಚಕ್ಕೆ ತರುತ್ತವೆ; ಅಲ್ಲಿ ಸಂಸ್ಥೆಗಳಿಗೆ ಸಾಮಾನ್ಯ ಲಾಭ ಮಾತ್ರ. ಬೇಡಿಕೆಗೆ ತಕ್ಕಂತೆ ಸಂಸ್ಥೆಗಳ ಸಂಖ್ಯೆ ಬದಲಾಗುತ್ತದೆ.

title.en: Shifts in demand with free entry and exit

body.en: Because the long-run supply curve is horizontal at min AC, a rise in demand does not change the equilibrium price; it raises the equilibrium quantity and the number of firms. A fall in demand lowers quantity and the number of firms, with price still equal to min AC. So with *free entry*, demand shifts have a larger effect on quantity and no effect on price, compared with a fixed number of firms.

points.en: *Demand* ↑ → same price, more output, more firms
*Demand* ↓ → same price, less output, fewer firms

problem.en: Market demand is qD = 1000 − 20p. All firms are identical, with minimum AC of ₹25 at an output of 20 units. With free entry and exit, find the equilibrium price, quantity and number of firms. What if demand becomes qD = 1200 − 20p?

steps.en: New demand: Q = 1200 − 500 = 700; n = 700/20 = 35 firms; price stays ₹25.

answer.en: p* = ₹25, Q* = 500, n = 25; after the demand rise, p* = ₹25, Q* = 700, n = 35.
